captions.text: class is hopelessly, permanently clouded over.
It's a great image for the futility of macro
forecasting. Joel Greenblat shares his favorite Howardism
in the book and it perfectly encapsulates this humility.
Experience is what you got when you didn't get
what you wanted. It's a brilliant quote.
What this means for you is that the I
know school of investing, the people who confidently go
on television and predict the exact path of interest
rates, the next quarter's GDP growth, or the outcome
of the next election, is incredibly dangerous to your
wealth. so dangerous. You must instead proudly
belong to the I don't know school.
Because you humbly accept that you don't know the
future, you are forced to manage your downside protection
so fiercely that the upside essentially takes care of
itself. Look at the generation of professional investors who
started their careers in the early 1980s and worked
all the way through the late 1990s.
Oh yeah. For nearly 17 years, fueled by
dropping interest rates and a massive economic expansion,
they never saw a market decline exceed 5%.
Incredible run it was.
But they were completely lulled to sleep.
They genuinely believe they knew the market only went
up. They lost all sight of risk because their
recent prolonged experience falsely taught them that systemic
risk simply didn't exist They confused a very
long, very pleasant economic cycle with a permanent
structural paradigm shift. Mhm.
And they paid for it dearly when the.com bubble
burst. But I have to ask, if we truly
can't know the future, if macro forecasting is mostly
a useless exercise in guessing, aren't we just
gambling blindly? I mean, why bother doing
any deep analysis at all if we just throw
our hands up and say, "Well, I don't know
what's going to happen." Because acknowledging macro uncertainty
forces you to focus hyperintensely on the micro realities
of the specific businesses you are buying.
